canonical_statement: The study evaluated whether large-scale propensity score models remain reliable for covariate balancing and bias reduction when fitted in small-sample settings representative of distributed data networks.
The study compared locally fitted LSPS models with a global LSPS model trained on the full dataset and with unadjusted outcome analyses.
The evaluation used the Merative MarketScan Commercial Claims and Encounters database and the Optum de-identified electronic health record dataset, both mapped to the OMOP common data model.

canonical_statement: Synthetic positive controls were generated from negative controls by adding simulated outcomes to create true hazard ratios of 1.5, 2, and 4.

Candidate target-comparator pairs were screened in CCAE using unadjusted single-regressor Cox models across negative control outcomes, and confounding bias was summarized with the lower bound of expected absolute systematic error (EASElb).
The authors characterized EASElb values from 0.0 to 0.1 as indicating little bias and values greater than 0.25 as indicating substantial bias.
In the unadjusted CCAE screening analysis, Losartan versus Hydrochlorothiazide had an EASElb of 0.26, estimated from 76 negative control outcomes.

canonical_statement: For each target-comparator pair, 20,000 eligible patients were randomly sampled and divided without replacement into 5 sites of 4,000, 10 sites of 2,000, 20 sites of 1,000, 40 sites of 500, or 80 sites of 250 patients.

Three analytic approaches were evaluated: a separate local LSPS model trained within each simulated site, one global LSPS model trained on the full population and applied to all sites, and an unadjusted analysis without propensity score adjustment.
Propensity scores were estimated with L1-regularized logistic regression, with the regularization hyperparameter selected by optimizing out-of-sample likelihood in 10-fold cross-validation.
Within each site, propensity score matching used 1:1 matching with a caliper of 0.2 on the logit scale.
Within each site, propensity score stratification divided patients into 10 equally sized strata.

For local analyses, propensity models and adjustment were performed separately within each simulated site; matching or stratification information was then pooled and a stratified Cox proportional hazards model was fitted to estimate the hazard ratio.

For global analyses, one propensity model was fitted on the full pooled population, its scores were applied to each site, and matching or stratification was still performed separately within each site before outcome modeling.

The study did not meta-analyze site-level treatment effect estimates; instead, it pooled person-level data across sites and conditioned the outcome models on site to isolate LSPS small-sample performance.
For propensity score stratification, site-specific strata were not merged, yielding k multiplied by 10 strata in the outcome model when k sites were simulated.
Residual systematic error was measured with EASE, the expected magnitude of bias estimated from negative control hazard-ratio estimates.
Precision was summarized as the geometric mean of inverse squared standard errors for log hazard-ratio estimates after empirical calibration using negative and positive controls.
Type I error was defined as rejection of the null for negative controls at alpha 0.05, and Type II error as failure to reject the null for synthetic positive controls at alpha 0.05.
The standard balance diagnostic was the maximum absolute standardized difference of means across covariates after sites were pooled.

The alternative balance diagnostic statistically tested whether standardized differences significantly exceeded 0.1 while accounting for sample size, and covariate-level balance could be combined by meta-analysis across sites.
The study fitted 1,872 propensity models across six target-comparator pairs, two databases, the full 20,000-patient samples, and all simulated site partitions.

canonical_statement: The SMD significance test identified fewer significantly unbalanced covariates than the standard maximum-SDM rule and did not cause all small-sample analyses to fail.
Meta-analyzing covariate balance across simulated sites further reduced the number of significantly unbalanced covariates for most target-comparator pairs.

Propensity score adjustment reduced EASE relative to unadjusted analyses in almost all scenarios; the stated exception was glimepiride versus saxagliptin in CCAE, where unadjusted EASE was already low.
Some comparisons retained substantial residual bias after adjustment, particularly nortriptyline versus fluoxetine in CCAE, and this residual bias increased as site sample size decreased.
The global propensity model sometimes reduced bias more effectively than local models, but the pattern was not strong or consistent across comparisons.
Propensity score matching generally produced lower EASE than stratification and only rarely produced EASE greater than 0.2.
Propensity score adjustment generally improved precision after empirical calibration, except for glimepiride versus saxagliptin in CCAE and losartan versus hydrochlorothiazide in Optum EHR.
The largest calibrated-precision gains were observed with propensity score stratification, especially when using the global LSPS model.
For nortriptyline versus fluoxetine and quinapril versus propranolol, calibrated-precision gains declined as site sample size decreased.
Type I error was generally controlled near the nominal 0.05 level across adjustment strategies, although variability was observed for quinapril versus propranolol in both databases.
Losartan versus hydrochlorothiazide was the only target-comparator pair with both low Type I and low Type II error for every adjustment strategy in both databases.
Power was generally low across comparisons and strategies, with Type II error frequently exceeding 0.25 to 0.50 even at the larger sample sizes.
The authors concluded that LSPS generally reduces confounding compared with no adjustment even in very small samples, unless the unadjusted comparison is already minimally confounded.
Local LSPS models generally performed similarly to the global LSPS model, suggesting little overall degradation from fitting high-dimensional propensity models on smaller local datasets.

The authors interpreted propensity score matching as superior for bias reduction but less precise than stratification; after empirical calibration, stratification may be preferred when its Type I error remains controlled.

The authors concluded that the standard maximum-SDM balance diagnostic is misleading in small samples and that the significance-based diagnostic is more robust because it accounts for chance imbalance.
The authors warned that relying only on standard SDM diagnostics may cause valid small-site data to be discarded even when LSPS substantially reduces systematic bias.
For comparisons with high residual bias after LSPS, the authors suggested incorporating prior confounder knowledge, applying dimensionality reduction, or using cardinality matching.
The simulated sites were random partitions of two large national databases and therefore did not reproduce real-site differences in populations, coding, prescribing, or geography.
Because the analysis did not use truly independent databases or real federated networks, generalizability to heterogeneous healthcare sites remains untested.
The analysis intentionally pooled person-level data rather than evaluating how meta-analysis of small or zero site-level counts might affect the overall treatment-effect estimate.
The analysis code was reported as publicly available in the OHDSI SmallSampleEstimationEvaluation GitHub repository and designed for datasets mapped to the OMOP common data model.
The study was supported by an unconditional Johnson & Johnson grant for methodological research (ICD 8593358).

Two authors were Johnson & Johnson employees and shareholders; the Erasmus University Medical Center research group received an institutional methodological-research grant from Johnson & Johnson; other authors disclosed related institutional contracts or outside grants.
Individual-level study data could not be shared publicly because of participant privacy, while aggregated supporting data could be made available on reasonable request to the corresponding author.
